title: LessonPlanner: Assisting Novice Teachers to Prepare Pedagogy-Driven Lesson Plans with Large Language Models
venue: UIST '24 (ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology)
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how novice teachers can efficiently prepare high-quality lesson plans, especially when they lack teaching experience and struggle to find suitable teaching materials and effective instructional strategies. The authors focus on whether large language models (LLMs) can support lesson planning in a structured, pedagogy-driven way rather than through an unstructured chat interface.

The paper presents LessonPlanner, a web-based system that guides users through lesson-goal setting and lesson-plan drafting using LLM-generated content. The system is structured around Bloom’s Taxonomy and Gagne’s Nine Events of Instruction, and it provides preset prompts, editable outline blocks, contextual LLM actions, and a markdown editor so users can refine or regenerate content. The design was informed by a formative study with six novice teachers and teaching assistants, and then evaluated in a within-subjects comparison against a baseline ChatGPT web interface.

The main evaluation involved 12 university students acting as teachers, preparing lesson plans for familiar data structures topics, followed by expert interviews with six teachers across university, primary, and high school contexts. Results showed that LessonPlanner improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans and reduced workload relative to the baseline. Participants especially valued the structured outline and pedagogy-aligned prompts, while also raising concerns about content accuracy and the need for human judgment. The study concludes that LLMs are more useful for lesson planning when embedded in an interactive, theory-informed workflow with flexible user control.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed HCI system paper with a within-subjects comparative study and expert interviews, but the evidence is primarily qualitative/UX-oriented with a small convenience sample and no reported effect sizes in the provided text. It is not a randomized K-12 efficacy trial.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows a useful improvement in teacher planning quality and reduced workload, but the measured effect is on planning artifacts and perceived effort rather than direct student learning outcomes. The impact appears modest and mostly on a specific novice-teacher population.

interventions.use_case: Interactive lesson-planning assistant powered by GPT-4 that generates lesson goals, outlines, pedagogically structured content, teaching activities, and refinements for novice K-12/university teachers.

finding.finding_summary: In a within-subjects study (n=12), LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of outcome lesson plans versus the baseline ChatGPT interface and reduced users' workload during lesson preparation. The paper also reports expert interviews (n=6) indicating the system was useful for making lesson planning more efficient by organizing content and suggesting relevant materials/strategies, but no numeric effect sizes or confidence intervals are provided in the text excerpt.
finding.measure: Lesson plan quality ratings by an expert teacher; NASA-TLX workload measures; SUS and trust questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: LessonPlanner significantly improved the quality of the resulting lesson plans compared with the baseline ChatGPT interface in a within-subjects study with 12 participants. Quality was judged by an experienced teacher using CIPP-inspired criteria covering alignment with learning objectives, useful materials, balance of theory/practice, effective strategies, and sufficient detail; the excerpt does not report the exact statistic or effect size.
finding.measure: Expert-rated lesson plan quality using CIPP-inspired criteria
